title: How Amnesia Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore amnesia, starting with the case of Clive Wearing, a musicologist whose memory resets every few seconds after viral encephalitis damaged his hippocampus and cortex. They walk through how memory works: sensory, short-term, and long-term memory, encoding, the hippocampus, amygdala and cortex roles, and long-term potentiation, plus memory types (episodic, procedural, semantic, emotional, spatial, working). They distinguish neurological amnesia (brain injury, stroke, drugs, alcohol, ECT) from dissociative amnesia (stress, cortisol, global vs. situational), define anterograde and retrograde amnesia and Ribot's law, discuss alcohol blackouts and Korsakoff syndrome, and cover coping strategies such as journals, habits, and smartphones. They also cover case studies (Clive Wearing, Henry Molaison H.M., Benjamin Kyle, a woman with a ceiling-fan injury), pop culture films, fugue states, signs to watch for, and research on erasing fear memories. The episode closes with a listener email correcting their description of termiticide and bait treatments.
topics: Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind

entities.name: Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind

segments.title: Opening banter and Clive Wearing introduction
segments.summary: The hosts joke about their memory and past episodes, then introduce Clive Wearing, a musicologist whose memory resets every few seconds, and Oliver Sacks' New Yorker profile of him, including journaling and the apple-core anecdote.

segments.title: Individual memory and HSAM
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how memory is highly individualized, with a side tangent on whether people see colors the same. They mention Mary Lou Henner's highly superior autobiographical memory (HSAM) and why forgetting is useful.

segments.title: How memory is formed: sensory, short-term, and long-term
segments.summary: The hosts explain the memory process: sensory memory, the nerve impulse and neurotransmitters crossing synapses, short-term memory, and encoding into long-term memory with the hippocampus, amygdala, thalamus, and cortex. They discuss long-term potentiation and emotion's role in memory strength.

segments.title: Types of long-term and working memory
segments.summary: The hosts list memory types: episodic (explicit), procedural (implicit), semantic (organized), emotional, spatial, and working memory, with examples like making coffee, favorite bands, and choosing from a menu. They note that emotion attaches to all memories and discuss neural plasticity.

segments.title: Neurological amnesia causes
segments.summary: Amnesia is described as a bad case of forgetting, often from brain injury. Causes listed include stroke, lack of oxygen, drugs, alcohol, blunt force trauma, and electroconvulsive therapy. The hosts explain Clive Wearing's herpes simplex encephalitis and the telephone-cord analogy for the hippocampus and cortex.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: A short break for sponsor messages before the show returns to dissociative amnesia.

segments.title: Dissociative amnesia and stress
segments.summary: The hosts describe dissociative amnesia, caused by intense stress and cortisol, which is usually temporary. They explain global versus situational subtypes, the brain blocking out traumatic events, and the rarity of fiction-style cases. A side tangent covers stress and cortisol in baby rhinos.

segments.title: Anterograde vs retrograde amnesia, alcohol blackouts, and Ribot's law
segments.summary: The hosts define anterograde amnesia (inability to form new memories) and retrograde amnesia (loss of past memories), with confabulation. They explain alcohol blackouts as anterograde amnesia and Ribot's law, where recent memories are lost first. They discuss speech loss from stroke and the hosts' grandfather's stroke.

segments.title: Living with amnesia, coping systems, and H.M.
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Clive Wearing's wife as caretaker, journals, sticky notes, habits, and smartphones as coping tools. They cover Henry Molaison (H.M.), whose hippocampus was removed to treat seizures, which showed that long-term memory is distinct from new memory formation. A woman's memoir about faking amnesia after a ceiling fan injury is also discussed.
